Researched the target repo. Findings first, because one of them shapes the whole PR.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- **phcc is a code generator, not a normal library.** `generate_phacc.py` does `shutil.rmtree("src/pytest_homeassistant_custom_component")` and rebuilds it by copying HA core's `tests/*.py` verbatim; `tests/conftest.py` becomes `plugins.py`, which is the sole `pytest11` entry point. The README says outright: *"PRs should not include changes to the `pytest_homeassistant_custom_component` files."* So a new fixture cannot just be added to `src/` — it would be erased on the next daily regen. It has to be added **by the generator**, and there's precedent: the generator already hand-patches `load_fixture`'s path resolution with line surgery, and `common.py`/`diagnostics` imports.
- **The scope argument is unusually strong, which matters for a repo whose stated goal is "the same functionality as the tests in home-assistant/core".** This isn't scope creep. Core's own tests *already* fail on these: both `report_usage` sites use `core_behavior=ERROR, core_integration_behavior=ERROR`. Only `custom_integration_behavior` defaults to `LOG`. So core gets this protection for free and a custom component structurally cannot — and phcc is the only project that serves custom components. The PR restores parity rather than adding a new idea.
- **phcc already reaches into the exact module we'd need.** Its autouse `reset_globals` calls `frame.async_setup(None)` and `frame._REPORTED_INTEGRATIONS.clear()`. That's both a precedent for touching `frame`, and the reason per-test detection is deterministic.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

One implementation question I resolved rather than asking, because the evidence is one-sided: **log handler, not patching `report_usage`.** Patching is both incomplete and semantically wrong — 10 modules do `from homeassistant.helpers.frame import ...` so a module-attribute patch misses them, and there's a call site that deliberately passes `custom_integration_behavior=ReportBehavior.IGNORE` that forcing `ERROR` would override. The log record already carries `at custom_components/x/__init__.py, line 460: <the source line>`, so the diagnostics lose almost nothing.

Three things that are genuinely your call:

questions.question: How should the fixture be enabled for phcc's users?

options.label: Non-autouse fixture + README snippet (Recommended)
options.description: Ship `no_deprecation_reports` as an ordinary fixture; users add a 3-line autouse wrapper in their own conftest. Exactly how phcc already documents the `snapshot` fixture. Zero risk to the ~100 dependents — nobody's suite changes until they opt in. Downside: undiscoverable unless you read the README.

options.label: Autouse, controlled by an ini option
options.description: `phcc_strict_deprecations = true` in pytest.ini/setup.cfg turns it on. More discoverable and a single switch per repo, but adds a config surface the maintainer has to own forever, and phcc has no ini options today — it would be the first.

options.label: Autouse by default
options.description: Strongest protection, and arguably the right default. But it would fail the suite of every dependent that currently has a deprecated call, arriving on a patch-version bump (their patch = routine HA update). Almost certainly rejected, and would earn phcc bug reports that aren't phcc's fault.

questions.question: How do we approach the maintainer?

options.label: Issue first, PR right after (Recommended)
options.description: Open an issue making the core-parity argument and naming the two placement options, then open the PR immediately referencing it. Costs nothing, gives Matthew a place to redirect the design before reviewing code, and the issue survives if the PR stalls. His own repo shows community PRs sitting open (#252, #255, #257).

options.label: PR only
options.description: Go straight to a PR with the argument in the description. Faster, and reviewable immediately. Risk: if he disagrees about placement or scope, the whole diff is wasted and the discussion happens under code instead of before it.

options.label: Issue only, wait for a reply
options.description: Propose it and build nothing until he responds. Lowest waste, but you asked for a PR and this delivers none.

questions.question: Should the PR include a test in phcc's own suite proving the fixture fires?

options.label: Yes — test with a deliberately deprecated call (Recommended)
options.description: Add a test that calls a deprecated helper from `tests/testing_config/custom_components/simple_integration` and asserts the fixture fails it, plus one asserting a clean test passes. Proves the thing works rather than asserting it does — and since the fixture is opt-in, it can't affect their other tests.

options.label: Yes, but assert on the log record only
options.description: Test the fixture against a synthetic log record instead of a real deprecated call. Simpler and won't break when HA removes the specific deprecated helper we picked, but it validates our own assumption about the message rather than the integration.

options.label: No test
options.description: Fixture and README only, smallest diff. Weakest — and this is a testing library, so an untested fixture is a poor argument for itself.

# Memory Index

- [Reader provider for #1414](project_reader_provider_1414.md) — design decisions (don't relitigate) + task state; worktree .worktrees/reader-provider

- [Test order: property → e2e → integration → unit](feedback_test_order_property_first.md) — broadest detector first; if you can't state a property, extract until you can
- [Code review every PR](feedback_review_every_pr.md) — every round so far found a real bug, including in PRs I called "provably inert"
- [Fallbacks need downstream reasoning](feedback_fallbacks_need_downstream_reasoning.md) — three times I reasoned about a fallback's own effect, not what the rest of the system did to the state it left
- [Tests must not build their own input contract](feedback_test_must_not_build_its_own_input_contract.md) — hand-built input validates your assumption, not the integration; cost a HIGH twice in one PR
- [Websocket `slots` = condition entities](project_websocket_slots_payload_is_condition_entities.md) — misleading field name; `slot_names` is the name map
- [v3 migration is a one-way door](project_v3_migration_one_way_door.md) — no code-level rollback; recovery is an HA backup restore, which dictates the live-test order

- [User-centric model (rev. 2026-08-18)](project_user_centric_model.md) — `users: {name: {...}}`; name is the user-facing identity but the SLOT NUMBER stays in identifiers as internal bookkeeping. Identifier-by-name (#1422) and never-reused handles both tried and reversed
- [project_matter_data_model.md](project_matter_data_model.md) — Future direction to formalize lock/user/PIN data model using Matter DoorLock cluster as reference architecture
- [project_credential_mgmt_refactor.md](project_credential_mgmt_refactor.md) — Approved design: migrate all providers onto unified User→Credential model (zwave_js accessControl + matter), seam at provider boundary, 1:1:1 UX

content.text: Picking up where I left off — the three things I flagged, now actually asked.

questions.question: How should the fixture be opted into? phcc has ~111 dependents, and their version strategy makes a patch bump an automatic HA update — so a failing autouse fixture would break other people's suites without warning.

options.label: Plain fixture + README snippet (Recommended)
options.description: Ship `no_deprecation_reports` as a normal (non-autouse) fixture. Users who want it everywhere add a 4-line autouse wrapper to their own conftest. Zero breakage for existing dependents, no new pytest machinery in a generated package, and it mirrors exactly how phcc already documents the `snapshot` fixture. Smallest thing a maintainer can say yes to.

options.label: Autouse, gated by an ini option
options.description: `phcc_fail_on_deprecation = true` in pytest config turns it on; autouse and failing once enabled. More discoverable and one behaviour, but needs a `pytest_addoption` hook injected into the generated package — more generator surface to maintain.

options.label: Autouse, warn by default
options.description: On for everyone but emits a warning rather than failing, with an opt-in to escalate. No breakage, but warnings in a test suite get ignored, which defeats the point — the bug in #1595 was already a warning nobody saw.

questions.question: Lead with a PR, or open an issue first? The README bounds scope to "the same functionality as the tests in home-assistant/core", and this exceeds that — though the parity argument is strong, since core callers already raise and only custom integrations get a silent log.

options.label: PR with the scope argument up front (Recommended)
options.description: Open the PR with a test proving it works, leading with the parity framing, and offer in the body to convert to a discussion if scope is the objection. A concrete reviewable diff beats an issue that sits — your own core#182808 has been waiting 9 days.

options.label: Issue first, PR after buy-in
options.description: Ask whether a phcc-authored fixture is in scope before writing generator code. Cheaper if Matthew says no, but slower and the idea is easier to dismiss in the abstract.

options.label: Both: issue, then PR immediately referencing it
options.description: Open the issue for the scope question and the PR right after so there's something to react to. Slight duplication, gives the maintainer an easy place to say "not in scope" without closing a PR.

questions.question: Where should the fixture live, given the generator does rmtree on src/ and rebuilds from HA core on every run?

options.label: Hand-authored module + 2nd entry point (Recommended)
options.description: Keep the fixture as a reviewable file outside src/, have the generator copy it in, and add a second `pytest11` entry point. The source of truth stays readable Python that a reviewer can diff, rather than line surgery. Would be phcc's first hand-authored module — a precedent Matthew may or may not want.

options.label: Generator appends it to plugins.py
options.description: Follows the existing `load_fixture` precedent exactly — the generator already patches the generated files with line surgery. No new packaging, no new entry point, but the fixture source lives as a string inside the generator and is harder to read and review.

options.label: Let the maintainer choose
options.description: Implement one, and say explicitly in the PR that the placement is the maintainer's call with the other option sketched. Risks a round trip, but placement is genuinely his architecture decision.

I've settled on making it autouse and gated by an ini option, filing an issue plus a referencing PR, and keeping it as a hand-authored module outside src/ that gets copied in by the generator with its own pytest11 entry point. Now I need to figure out exactly where this file should live—maybe a top-level extras directory or somewhere inside the generator package itself.

I'll place the file at `extras/deprecation.py` in the repo root since `find_packages(where="src")` only packages src anyway, and the generator can copy it into the compiled package directory. I need to be careful about ordering though—the generator adds a provenance docstring to every .py file under the package directory, so I should copy my file in after that loop runs, letting it keep its own docstring instead of a false attribution note. I'm also working out the entry point registration in setup.py for the new pytest11 plugin.

But this raises a question: since the repo's `src/` tree is committed and CI regenerates it before tests, I need to check the GitHub Actions workflow to confirm the generated file will exist before the entry point is exercised. For the plugin itself, I'm thinking through the interface—defining `pytest_addoption` to register an ini option, plus an autouse fixture that checks that config value, and settling on a name like `phcc_strict_deprecations` for the option.

I'm leaning toward a single boolean ini option, `phcc_fail_on_deprecation_report` (default false), rather than adding a domain-filtering option too. The concern is false positives from mock/test integrations under `custom_components` in consumer test suites—like LCM's MockLCMLock fixtures—that aren't the actual custom integration being tested, so I'm weighing whether to punt that filtering to a follow-up rather than building it into this first pass.

Now I'm thinking through whether to add a second option, `phcc_deprecation_domains`, to scope which domains trigger the failure, since it's cheap to implement and useful for repos loading third-party integrations in tests—balancing that against keeping the surface area small for maintainers to accept. I'm also working out how to actually detect a custom integration from the log record itself, since the deprecation warning message format embeds the domain and file location in a specific string pattern I'll need to parse.

Actually, parsing the rendered message text is fragile — instead I realize the logger call passes structured arguments, so `record.args` directly contains the integration type prefix and domain name rather than requiring text parsing, which aligns with preferring structured data checks over string assertions.

I'm checking that both log call sites use the same argument order (integration_type, then domain), confirming this approach works consistently across both, and I'm noting there's a third relevant log call nearby to also verify.

I'm now considering the detection logic itself: rather than just checking `record.args[0] == "custom "`, which is fragile against future shape changes, I want a fallback that still catches the case by checking if the message text starts with "Detected that custom integration" even if the args don't match expectations—so the fixture doesn't silently break if internals shift.

Simplicity for reviewers matters, so I'll make the message-prefix check the primary detection method since it's the stable, user-visible contract, and use `record.args[1]` for domain filtering only when args are present. Next I want to check the CI workflow ordering around tests/generation, and verify whether `src/` is actually committed in the repo.

I'm tracing the CI sequence for a PR: checkout, install package, regenerate with the flag, reinstall, then run tests. """
Fail tests whose run makes Home Assistant report a custom integration.

Unlike everything under ``pytest_homeassistant_custom_component``, this module
is written here rather than extracted from homeassistant/core. It exists
because core cannot supply it: ``report_usage`` raises for core callers and for
callers with no integration frame, and only *custom* integrations get
``ReportBehavior.LOG``. A custom integration therefore has no way to learn
from its own test suite that it called a deprecated API -- the report goes to a
log nobody reads until a user pastes it into an issue, by which time the
removal version may already be close.

Off unless ``phacc_fail_on_deprecation_report`` is set, so adding it breaks
nobody's suite on an automatic version bump.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from collections.abc import Generator
import logging

import pytest

# Every report Home Assistant makes about an integration is formatted by one of
# two ``_LOGGER.log`` calls in ``homeassistant.helpers.frame``, and both pass
# the integration kind first and the domain second. Reading those two arguments
# keeps this off the rendered wording, which is not a contract and has been
# reworded before.
_FRAME_LOGGER = "homeassistant.helpers.frame"
_KIND_ARG = 0
_DOMAIN_ARG = 1
_CUSTOM_KIND = "custom "

_INI_ENABLED = "phacc_fail_on_deprecation_report"
_INI_DOMAINS = "phacc_deprecation_report_domains"


def pytest_addoption(parser: pytest.Parser) -> None:
    """Register the ini options that enable and narrow the check."""
    parser.addini(
        _INI_ENABLED,
        "Fail a test if Home Assistant reports a custom integration for "
        "deprecated or incorrect API usage. Off by default.",
        type="bool",
        default=False,
    )
    parser.addini(
        _INI_DOMAINS,
        "Domains to fail on, one per line. Empty means every custom "
        "integration, which is what a repository holding one integration "
        "wants; name domains only if the tests deliberately load somebody "
        "else's custom integration too.",
        type="linelist",
        default=[],
    )


class _ReportCollector(logging.Handler):
    """Collect the reports that blame a custom integration under test."""

    def __init__(self, domains: frozenset[str]) -> None:
        """Watch ``domains``, or every custom integration when it is empty."""
        super().__init__()
        self._domains = domains

"""Tests for the deprecation-report fixture."""

import pytest

# A module inside a `custom_components/` path, which is the only thing that
# makes Home Assistant call a frame a custom integration's
# (`frame.get_integration_frame` matches on the path, nothing else). Written to
# disk rather than imported so the test does not depend on a real integration
# staying deprecated.
PROBE = '''
from homeassistant.helpers.frame import ReportBehavior, report_usage


def call_deprecated_api():
    """Report from a frame inside custom_components, as a real one would."""
    report_usage(
        "calls something deprecated",
        core_behavior=ReportBehavior.IGNORE,
        core_integration_behavior=ReportBehavior.IGNORE,
        custom_integration_behavior=ReportBehavior.LOG,
        breaks_in_ha_version="2099.1.0",
    )
'''

TEST_USING_PROBE = '''
from custom_components.probe_integration.probe import call_deprecated_api


def test_calls_deprecated_api():
    call_deprecated_api()
'''


@pytest.fixture
def probe(pytester: pytest.Pytester) -> None:
    """Lay down the custom integration and the test that calls into it."""
    probe_dir = pytester.path / "custom_components" / "probe_integration"
    probe_dir.mkdir(parents=True)
    (probe_dir.parent / "__init__.py").write_text("")
    (probe_dir / "__init__.py").write_text("")
    (probe_dir / "probe.py").write_text(PROBE)
    pytester.makepyfile(test_probe=TEST_USING_PROBE)


def test_off_by_default(pytester: pytest.Pytester, probe: None) -> None:
    """An integration that adds the package does not inherit a failing suite.

    The whole reason this is opt-in: phacc tracks homeassistant releases with
    patch bumps, so anything on by default would break dependents' suites on
    an automatic update.
    """
    pytester.makeini("[pytest]\n")
    pytester.runpytest_subprocess().assert_outcomes(passed=1)

The mechanism works—file, line, and source are surfaced correctly. But since pytest.fail in a fixture's teardown after yield produces an ERROR rather than a FAILURE, same as in LCM, my assertions need to check for passed=1, errors=1 instead of failed=1.

That raises a design question: is a teardown error acceptable, or should this register as a true failure? Getting a real failure instead would mean hooking into the call phase itself, like wrapping pytest_runtest_call, which is heavier machinery but gives a proper failure signal. I'm weighing whether raising after yield in that hookwrapper actually registers as a call-phase failure, since hookwrapper semantics discourage that pattern while the newer wrapper mechanism might allow it.

Modern pytest's wrapper mode does let you raise and have it propagate as the actual test outcome, giving a clean FAILED result instead of a confusing "passed but errored" report — and I think that confusion is worth avoiding even at the cost of extra complexity, so I'm leaning toward implementing the hook wrapper version since it's only about fifteen lines and produces clearly better output than the fixture-based teardown-error approach.

I'm sketching out a `pytest_runtest_call` hook using wrapper mode: it checks if the feature is enabled via the ini setting, attaches a log collector before yielding control to run the actual test, then removes the handler and restores the logging level afterward, and if the collector caught anything it calls `pytest.fail` to turn that into a genuine test failure. Now I need to be careful about the case where the test itself already failed during the yield — the wrapper needs to preserve that original failure rather than masking it with the log-based failure.

With a bare `try/finally`, if the test raises, the exception propagates right past the trailing `pytest.fail` check, so the genuine failure wins and reports from an already-failed test just get silently dropped, which is the correct behavior since the test failed anyway. I'm also noting that this wrapper only covers the call phase, not setup, so deprecated logging calls happening during fixture setup wouldn't be caught here.

Since real integration work often happens in setup fixtures rather than the test body itself, I need the hook to wrap all three phases—setup, call, teardown—not just call, otherwise there's a meaningful coverage gap. The tricky part is that failures during setup are reported as errors, not failures, so I need a design that collects records across setup and call but asserts once at the right point to get consistent failure reporting.

Reconsidering the autouse-fixture approach: it isn't guaranteed to run before every other fixture since autouse ordering only guarantees precedence over non-autouse fixtures at the same scope, not a strict global ordering. Still, in practice this fixture would run early enough to catch most setup activity, though any resulting issue would surface as a teardown error rather than a clean failure — a tradeoff versus the hook-based approach, which yields cleaner output.

Since this is a PR into someone else's repository, I want to pick whichever approach has the best behavior-to-complexity ratio and be upfront about the tradeoff. I'll go with hook wrappers on setup and call using stash-based state, roughly 25 lines, since it properly covers both phases and reports as a real failure rather than a teardown artifact — worth the modest extra code. Sketching this out: a setup hook that attaches the handler and stores collector/logger state in item.stash without detaching, followed by a call hook that continues from there.

But I realize setup can error or skip without call ever running, so I also need a teardown wrapper to guarantee detachment happens regardless. It's a bit fiddly but workable, though it makes me wonder whether there's a cleaner model — like how pytest's own `filterwarnings = error` converts warnings to errors right at emission time, giving a much better failure experience by pointing directly at the offending call rather than surfacing later. I'm now considering whether the log handler could raise immediately when it captures a matching record, rather than deferring the failure to a later hook.

A handler raising inside `emit` doesn't actually propagate, though — logging catches exceptions there via `handleError`, so that path is a dead end regardless of `raiseExceptions`. Instead, the cleaner approach is to patch the two private helper functions in `frame.py` that get called via module-level lookup, since IGNORE filtering already happens before they're invoked, so the semantics stay intact — this just adds two more private names to an already-existing pattern of touching internals like `_REPORTED_INTEGRATIONS`.

But there's a real gap: broad `except Exception` blocks scattered throughout the integration's own code could silently swallow a raised deprecation error, letting a test pass when it shouldn't — and that's more dangerous than a teardown failure because it's invisible. Given how many broad exception handlers this particular integration has, that risk feels significant enough to weigh seriously against the approach.

So I'm leaning toward keeping the fixture-based log collection since it can't be swallowed, accepting the teardown-error tradeoff, and just being clearer in the message about where it surfaces. I want to check whether there's a way to get proper failure semantics without adding hook complexity, but for now let me actually assess whether the setup-phase gap is even a practical concern with an autouse function-scoped fixture.

Since autouse fixtures are prioritized ahead of other function-scoped fixtures, my fixture already covers setup for nearly everything, and teardown errors still fail CI loudly enough. So I'll finalize on keeping the fixture, updating tests to expect the errors=1 result, and documenting the teardown semantics honestly rather than chasing a more complex alternative.

I do notice there's actually a strong in-repo precedent for this exact pattern — another fixture already fails tests via `pytest.fail` in its after-yield teardown phase for a similar mock-detection problem — which reinforces that raising during teardown is the idiomatic approach here rather than something hacky.

Home Assistant reports deprecated and incorrect API usage through
`homeassistant.helpers.frame.report_usage`. That report *raises* for a
homeassistant/core caller and for a call made straight from a test, but for a
custom integration it only *logs*. A custom integration's test suite therefore
stays green while its production code calls something Home Assistant has already
scheduled for removal, and the warning is only seen once a user pastes a log into
an issue.

Set `phacc_fail_on_deprecation_report` to turn those reports into test failures:

```ini
[pytest]
asyncio_mode = auto
phacc_fail_on_deprecation_report = true
```

and the source line that triggered it:

domains you are responsible for so only your own reports fail the suite:

```ini
phacc_deprecation_report_domains =
    my_integration
```

content.text: Opening the issue first, as decided:

input.command:
gh issue create --repo MatthewFlamm/pytest-homeassistant-custom-component --title "Optional check: fail a test when Home Assistant reports the custom integration for deprecated API usage" --body "$(cat <<'BODY'
## The gap

`homeassistant.helpers.frame.report_usage` is how Home Assistant tells a caller it used a deprecated or incorrect API. It takes a separate behaviour per kind of caller, and the asymmetry is the problem:

| caller | behaviour | result in a test |
| --- | --- | --- |
| homeassistant/core | `core_behavior` — `ERROR` at most call sites | raises |
| a test frame, no integration in the stack | `core_behavior` via `MissingIntegrationFrame` | raises |
| **a custom integration** | `custom_integration_behavior` — **defaults to `LOG`** | logs, test passes |

So core gets this protection for free in its own test suite, and a custom integration structurally cannot. Its production code can call a deprecated helper, the suite stays green at 100% coverage, and the only place the warning ever appears is a user's log — typically pasted into an issue some months later, possibly after the removal version has been decided.

## A concrete case

I hit this in [lock_code_manager#1595](https://github.com/raman325/lock_code_manager/issues/1595). An earlier PR had migrated every `device_registry.async_get_device` call to `async_get_device_by_identifier`. A later PR branched before that landed and added a new migration block containing the old calls, so the merge had nothing to conflict with. The suite was green, there was a dedicated test asserting the exact end state that block produces, and that test passed — because the code was *correct*, just scheduled for removal in 2027.8. A user found it by reading their own logs.

I added a local fixture that watches the log and fails the test. It caught it immediately, and it seems like something every integration using this package would want rather than something each of us reimplements.

## Why here and not in home-assistant/core

Core's own callers already raise, so core has no reason to add this — there is nothing there for it to catch. The gap exists only for custom integrations, and this package is the only thing that serves them. I'd argue that makes it *parity* work rather than a new idea, even though the code itself isn't extracted from core.

## Sketch

- Off unless `phacc_fail_on_deprecation_report = true`, so it cannot change an existing dependent's suite result on an automatic version bump.
- A log handler on `homeassistant.helpers.frame` rather than patching `report_usage`. Patching would be both incomplete and wrong: ~10 modules do `from homeassistant.helpers.frame import report_usage` so a module-attribute patch misses them, and at least one call site deliberately passes `custom_integration_behavior=ReportBehavior.IGNORE`, which forcing `ERROR` would override. A handler also cannot be swallowed by a broad `except Exception` in the integration under test, which a raised exception can.
- Reports are identified from `record.args` (the kind and the domain, which both `_LOGGER.log` call sites pass in the same positions) rather than by matching the rendered wording.
- Fails from after the fixture's `yield`, the same shape `reset_globals` already uses to fail a test that serialized a mock object.

## The question

`src/pytest_homeassistant_custom_component` is wiped and regenerated, and the README says PRs should not touch it — so this needs a home the generator writes. I have it working as a hand-authored module under `extras/` that `generate_phacc.py` copies into the package after generation, plus a second `pytest11` entry point. That would be the first module in the package not extracted from core, which is a precedent you may or may not want.

Happy to rework the placement, or to drop it if this is outside what you want the package to be. Opening a PR right behind this so there is something concrete to react to.
BODY
)" 2>&1 | tail -3

Add an opt-in check that fails on deprecation reports (#258)

`report_usage` raises for homeassistant/core callers and for calls made
from a test frame, but `custom_integration_behavior` defaults to `LOG`.
A custom integration therefore cannot learn from its own suite that it
called a deprecated API: the report goes only to a log, which is usually
read months later by a user filing an issue.

Off unless `phacc_fail_on_deprecation_report` is set, so no dependent's
suite changes result on an automatic version bump.

A log handler rather than a patch of `report_usage`, which would be both
incomplete and wrong: ~10 modules bind it by name so a module-attribute
patch misses them, and a call site that deliberately passes
`custom_integration_behavior=ReportBehavior.IGNORE` would be overridden.
A handler also survives a broad `except Exception` in the code under
test, which a raised exception does not. Reports are recognised from
`record.args`, where both call sites pass the integration kind and domain
in the same positions, so the check does not depend on the wording.

The module is authored here rather than extracted from core, so it lives
in `extras/` and the generator copies it into the package after the loop
that stamps core's provenance on everything. A second `pytest11` entry
point loads it. The generated copy is committed because `publish.yml`
builds from the checkout without regenerating, and a declared entry point
to a missing module would break pytest startup for every consumer.

from pathlib import Path

d = Path("/Users/raman/.claude/projects/-Users-raman-projects-lock-code-manager/memory")

(d / "feedback_deprecation_reports_need_a_detector.md").write_text('''---
name: feedback_deprecation_reports_need_a_detector
description: "When a framework reports a problem only by logging it, no assertion or coverage number can catch it — the detector has to watch the log, in the place the warning actually appears"
metadata:
  type: feedback
---

Issue #1595: a released version called three device-registry APIs Home Assistant
removes in 2027.8. The suite was at 100% coverage, there was a test dedicated to
that exact code block, and it passed — because the code was *correct*, just
scheduled for removal. A user found it by reading their own logs.

**Why nothing caught it:** `report_usage` raises for homeassistant/core callers
and for calls made from a test frame, but `custom_integration_behavior` defaults
to `LOG`. The warning existed, in the one place the test suite was not looking.

**How to apply:**

- When a framework's only signal for a class of problem is a log line, the
  detector goes on the log. Build it as an autouse fixture so it covers the
  whole suite at once rather than a per-call assertion, which only ever covers
  the call you thought of. Same instinct as
  [[feedback_test_order_property_first]]: the broadest detector first.
- Recognise records by their `args`, not their rendered text. Wording is not a
  contract; the argument positions usually are. See [[feedback_caplog_checks]].
- **Prefer collecting the log to patching the reporter into raising.** A raised
  exception gets swallowed by any broad `except Exception` between the call and
  the test — and integrations are full of those — so the check would silently
  pass. A log record cannot be swallowed.
- Ask whether the gap is mine or everyone's. This one was structural for every
  custom integration, so it went upstream too:
  MatthewFlamm/pytest-homeassistant-custom-component#258 / #259, see
  [[reference_phcc_is_a_generator]].
''')

idx = d / "MEMORY.md"
lines = idx.read_text().rstrip("\n")
add = "- [Deprecation reports need a detector](feedback_deprecation_reports_need_a_detector.md) — a warning that only logs is invisible to coverage and assertions; watch the log, and collect it rather than making it raise"
if "feedback_deprecation_reports_need_a_detector" not in lines:
    lines += "\n" + add + "\n"
idx.write_text(lines)
print("written + indexed")
PY

content.text:
Both are up: issue [#258](https://github.com/MatthewFlamm/pytest-homeassistant-custom-component/issues/258) and PR [#259](https://github.com/MatthewFlamm/pytest-homeassistant-custom-component/pull/259), following your three decisions (ini-gated autouse, issue-then-PR, hand-authored module + second entry point).

## What shipped

| file | why |
|---|---|
| `extras/deprecation.py` | the plugin: 2 ini options, 1 autouse fixture |
| `generate_phacc/{const,generate_phacc}.py` | copies it in **after** the loop that stamps core's provenance, so it keeps its own docstring; `extras` kept separate from `files`, which is core's list |
| `src/…/deprecation.py` | the generated copy — see below |
| `setup.py` | second `pytest11` entry point |
| `tests/test_deprecation.py` | 5 `pytester` tests |
| `README.md`, `setup.cfg` | docs, plus the option enabled for phcc's own suite |

**Verified:** full phcc suite green, 12 passed, with the option turned on for the repo itself (so `simple_integration` is provably clean). The five tests cover off-by-default, on-and-failing with the file/line in the message, a non-custom report being ignored, and the domain filter both narrowing and matching.

## Three things worth knowing

**CI has not run.** It came back `conclusion=action_required` — first-time-contributor PRs need Matthew to approve workflow runs. Since CI's regeneration step is the one part of my change I could not execute locally (the generator clones home-assistant/core in full), that verification is still outstanding. I validated the paths resolve from the repo root the way the workflows invoke it, and said so explicitly in the PR rather than implying it was tested.

**I committed a generated file the README says not to touch,** and the reason is load-bearing: `publish.yml` runs `setup.py sdist bdist_wheel` on a plain checkout with *no* regeneration step. An entry point declared in `setup.py` pointing at a file only the generator produces would break pytest startup for every consumer of the published wheel. Flagged in the PR as his call.

**Your open PR #1604 had a wrong claim, now fixed forward** (commit `51dc9cad`). I'd written that HA's per-call-site dedup means only the first test to hit a reintroduced call fails. It doesn't — phcc's autouse `reset_globals` clears `frame._REPORTED_INTEGRATIONS` after every test. Proven by re-running the mutation across both migration tests: both error, not one.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- I rejected the more elegant implementation for a concrete reason worth remembering: patching `report_usage` to raise would give a traceback at the call site, but **any broad `except Exception` between the call and the test would swallow it** — and LCM's provider layer is full of those. A log record can't be swallowed. The uglier mechanism is the more reliable detector.
- Reading `record.args` rather than the message text matters more than it looks: both `_LOGGER.log` sites in `frame.py` pass the integration kind and domain in the same two positions, and that ordering is far more stable than the wording, which HA has already reworded once.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

The phcc clone lives at `/Users/raman/projects/pytest-homeassistant-custom-component` with its own `.venv` and the branch checked out, if you want to poke at it. Want me to also wire the ini option into lock_code_manager's `setup.cfg` and delete the local fixture, contingent on #259 landing — or leave the local copy until it does?

content.thinking:
Now it's clear: PR #1273 pins pytest to an exact version that conflicts with requirements_test.txt's floor, making the constraint unsatisfiable until HA core itself upgrades. This has been open and conflicting since June 19, and Dependabot has no way to resolve it on its own.

#1588 has the same shape—HA pins zeroconf to one version while dependabot wants a slightly newer one. The real fix seems twofold: stop declaring packages whose version is dictated by phcc/HA in the first place, since declaring pytest in requirements_test.txt invites dependabot to bump it past what phcc allows. I'm trying to figure out why zeroconf is declared at all, since it's a core HA dependency already pinned via package_constraints—unlike zha, zigpy, matter, or esphome deps, which genuinely need explicit declarations since HA doesn't install those extras by default.

The second piece is telling dependabot to ignore the HA-pinned packages so it stops opening unmergeable PRs. I'm weighing whether to add ignore entries for those while keeping the group for packages that should move together with HA, but that risks never bumping zha/zigpy/etc. even though they need to track HA's own bumps for LCM tests to stay valid. The phcc PR needs updating: it should default to on rather than off, since that's a good breaking change, and the patching mechanism should be simplified to avoid heavy generator boilerplate. But I'm still mid-task on the LCM dependency work, which is nearly finished, so I should wrap that up first — lint, commit, push, and open the PR — before pivoting to phcc.

Now let me think through the simplification properly, since it's the real design question. The current setup has a lot of moving parts: a deprecation module, a generator copy, const.py entries, a second entry point, and a committed generated file. A cleaner alternative would be to put the fixture in a separate top-level package under src/ that the rmtree-based cleanup never touches, since setup.py's package discovery picks up anything under src/ anyway — so a hand-written, never-regenerated module with its own entry point could sidestep the whole regeneration problem.

That approach would eliminate the extras directory, the const.py additions, the generator change, and the oddity of committing a generated copy, leaving just one new hand-written package plus one entry-point line. The naming is a bit awkward though — something like a second top-level package name feels unusual, though it's not unprecedented since distributions do sometimes ship multiple top-level packages. I'm also considering whether there's an even simpler route, like declaring the plugin purely through setup.py without a conftest at all.

Actually the cleanest path is making it a single top-level module rather than a package — one file plus two setup.py lines, with no generator changes needed at all, since `package_dir` already maps root to `src`. Weighing this bare-module approach against a full package, the module route feels more minimal and distinctive enough as a name not to feel like pollution.

I'm checking that the generator's docstring-stamping loop and its `rmtree` call only touch `PACKAGE_DIR`, so this new standalone file stays untouched by either. That settled, I'm now thinking through the first real design decision: whether the deprecation warning feature should be on by default, which would mean removing a related config option.

Raman wants it on by default since it's a good breaking change, but I should keep an escape hatch for people who can't fix everything right away — simplest approach is keeping the same boolean option name but just flipping its default to `True`, so it reads naturally as an opt-out rather than adding a new inverted flag. ## Proposed change

Supersedes #1588 and #1273. Neither could ever have gone green: both failed at `uv pip install`, before a single test ran, because dependabot raised a version that something already pins exactly.

### #1588 — one member of the group was the problem

```
Because homeassistant>=2026.9.4 depends on zeroconf==0.151.1 and you require
homeassistant>=2026.9.4, we can conclude that you require zeroconf==0.151.1.
And because you require zeroconf==0.151.3, your requirements are unsatisfiable.
```

I checked the `homeassistant` wheel's `Requires-Dist` against all sixteen packages in the `homeassistant` dependabot group. It constrains exactly one of them:

| | constrained by the homeassistant wheel |
| --- | --- |
| `zeroconf` | **yes — `zeroconf==0.151.1`** |
| the other 15 (`zha`, `zigpy`, `matter-python-client`, `zwave-js-server-python`, …) | no — integration deps, pinned in manifests we have to mirror ourselves |

Nothing in this repo imports `zeroconf`; the pin dates to #77. So our copy could only ever agree with HA or contradict it, and it contradicted it. Removed — the resolver now picks `zeroconf==0.151.1` up from HA on its own, which I confirmed. The other seven updates are taken as dependabot proposed them.

### #1273 — not fixable, only ignorable

```
Because pytest-homeassistant-custom-component==0.13.346 depends on pytest==9.0.3
and you require pytest>=9.1.1, your requirements are unsatisfiable.
```

phacc pins pytest **exactly**, because it carries the whole of HA core's test requirements. It was 9.0.3 then and it is still 9.0.3 on the latest release (0.13.367). Raising our floor past that pin cannot resolve however long the PR stays open, which is why #1273 sat conflicting for three months. An `ignore` entry in `dependabot.yaml` is the only thing that stops it being reopened; phacc brings pytest forward on its own schedule and our `>=9.0.3` floor keeps working when it does.

## Type of change

- [x] Dependency upgrade
- [ ] Bugfix (non-breaking change which fixes an issue)
- [ ] New feature (which adds functionality)
- [ ] Breaking change (fix/feature causing existing functionality to break)
- [ ] Code quality improvements to existing code or addition of tests

## Additional information

- This PR fixes or closes issue: supersedes #1588 and #1273 (both should close themselves once dependabot re-evaluates; worth a glance in case they need closing by hand)

Resolved set verified in a clean venv — `homeassistant==2026.9.4`, `zeroconf==0.151.1` (from HA), `zha==2.2.2`, `zigpy==2.2.0`, `zha-quirks==2.2.2`, `aioesphomeapi==46.6.0`, `debugpy==1.8.22`, `phacc==0.13.367`. Full suite green against it: **2450 passed, 3 skipped**. zigpy 2.2.0 changes struct bitfield endianness, so the ZHA provider tests were the risk; they pass.

One thing left alone deliberately: `tests/providers/zha/conftest.py:345` uses `zigpy.quirks.get_device`, which now warns that it moved to `zhaquirks.legacy` — 77 warnings in the run. Pre-existing, unrelated to the resolution failures, happy to do it separately.

I'm also updating the tests for default-on behavior with an opt-out test, adjusting imports, and reframing the README around the new default. I'm keeping the ini option name positive (documenting `= false` to disable, similar to filterwarnings) rather than renaming it.

One nagging worry is that putting this as a new top-level `phacc_deprecation` module introduces a new public name in site-packages rather than keeping it inside the package namespace — the maintainer might prefer it nested, but nesting it inside the package means it'd get wiped by regeneration, so the top-level module seems like the simpler tradeoff.

I considered a namespace-style layout to avoid the new top-level name, but that seems worse, so I'll stick with the top-level module and just explain the tradeoff in the PR description. I also need to remember not to amend the existing commit since the PR is already created — I should add these changes as a second commit on the same branch and push forward rather than rewriting history.

Now I'll revert the generator files back to their origin/master state by checking out `generate_phacc/const.py` and `generate_phacc/generate_phacc.py` explicitly with named paths, then remove the two deprecation.py copies as a first concrete step.

"""
Fail tests whose run makes Home Assistant report a custom integration.

Unlike `pytest_homeassistant_custom_component`, this module is written here
rather than extracted from homeassistant/core, and it lives beside that package
rather than inside it because the generator rebuilds that directory from
scratch on every run.

It exists because core cannot supply it: `report_usage` raises for core callers
and for callers with no integration frame, and only *custom* integrations get
`ReportBehavior.LOG`. A custom integration therefore has no way to learn from
its own test suite that it called a deprecated API -- the report goes to a log
nobody reads until a user pastes it into an issue, by which time the removal
version may be close.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from collections.abc import Generator
import logging

import pytest

# Every report Home Assistant makes about an integration is formatted by one of
# two `_LOGGER.log` calls in `homeassistant.helpers.frame`, and both pass the
# integration kind first and the domain second. Reading those two arguments
# keeps this off the rendered wording, which is not a contract and has been
# reworded before.
_FRAME_LOGGER = "homeassistant.helpers.frame"
_KIND_ARG = 0
_DOMAIN_ARG = 1
_CUSTOM_KIND = "custom "

_INI_ENABLED = "phacc_fail_on_deprecation_report"
_INI_DOMAINS = "phacc_deprecation_report_domains"


def pytest_addoption(parser: pytest.Parser) -> None:
    """Register the ini options that disable and narrow the check."""
    parser.addini(
        _INI_ENABLED,
        "Fail a test if Home Assistant reports a custom integration for "
        "deprecated or incorrect API usage. On by default; set false to "
        "silence it while working through a backlog of reports.",
        type="bool",
        default=True,
    )
    parser.addini(
        _INI_DOMAINS,
        "Domains to fail on, one per line. Empty means every custom "
        "integration, which is what a repository holding one integration "
        "wants; name domains only if the tests deliberately load somebody "
        "else's custom integration too.",
        type="linelist",
        default=[],
    )


class _ReportCollector(logging.Handler):
    """Collect the reports that blame a custom integration under test."""

    def __init__(self, domains: frozenset[str]) -> None:
        """Watch `domains`, or every custom integration when it is empty."""
        super().__init__()
        self._domains = domains
        self.reports: list[str] = []

    def emit(self, record: logging.LogRecord) -> None:
        """Keep `record` if it is a report about a watched integration."""
        args = record.args
        if not isinstance(args, tuple) or len(args) <= _DOMAIN_ARG:
            return
        if args[_KIND_ARG] != _CUSTOM_KIND:
            return
        if self._domains and args[_DOMAIN_ARG] not in self._domains:
            return
        self.reports.append(record.getMessage())


@pytest.fixture(autouse=True)
def fail_on_deprecation_report(request: pytest.FixtureRequest) -> Generator[None]:
    """
    Turn Home Assistant's reports about this integration into test failures.

    Reports name the file, the line and the source line that triggered them,
    so the failure says where to look without a traceback.

    Every test that reaches a reported call fails, not only the first: Home
    Assistant deduplicates reports by call site, but `reset_globals` clears
    that set after each test, so each test starts able to see its own.
    """
    if not request.config.getini(_INI_ENABLED):
        yield
        return

    collector = _ReportCollector(frozenset(request.config.getini(_INI_DOMAINS)))
    logger = logging.getLogger(_FRAME_LOGGER)
    # Reports are logged at WARNING. A suite that raised the threshold above it
    # would otherwise get a check that silently passes forever, which is worse
    # than not having one.
    restore_level = logger.level if not logger.isEnabledFor(logging.WARNING) else None
    if restore_level is not None:
        logger.setLevel(logging.WARNING)
    logger.addHandler(collector)
    try:
        yield
    finally:
        logger.removeHandler(collector)
        if restore_level is not None:
            logger.setLevel(restore_level)

    if collector.reports:
        pytest.fail(
            "Home Assistant reported this integration for deprecated or "
            "incorrect API usage:\n\n" + "\n\n".join(collector.reports),
            pytrace=False,
        )

"""
Fail tests whose run makes Home Assistant report a custom integration.

Unlike `pytest_homeassistant_custom_component`, this module is written here
rather than extracted from homeassistant/core, and it lives beside that package
rather than inside it because the generator rebuilds that directory from
scratch on every run.

It exists because core cannot supply it: `report_usage` raises for core callers
and for callers with no integration frame, and only *custom* integrations get
`ReportBehavior.LOG`. A custom integration therefore has no way to learn from
its own test suite that it called a deprecated API -- the report goes to a log
nobody reads until a user pastes it into an issue, by which time the removal
version may be close.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from collections.abc import Generator
import logging

import pytest

# Every report Home Assistant makes about an integration is formatted by one of
# two `_LOGGER.log` calls in `homeassistant.helpers.frame`, and both pass the
# integration kind first and the domain second. Reading those two arguments
# keeps this off the rendered wording, which is not a contract and has been
# reworded before.
_FRAME_LOGGER = "homeassistant.helpers.frame"
_KIND_ARG = 0
_DOMAIN_ARG = 1
_CUSTOM_KIND = "custom "

_INI_ENABLED = "phacc_fail_on_deprecation_report"
_INI_DOMAINS = "phacc_deprecation_report_domains"


def pytest_addoption(parser: pytest.Parser) -> None:
    """Register the ini options that disable and narrow the check."""
    parser.addini(
        _INI_ENABLED,
        "Fail a test if Home Assistant reports a custom integration for "
        "deprecated or incorrect API usage. On by default; set false to "
        "silence it while working through a backlog of reports.",
        type="bool",
        default=True,
    )
    parser.addini(
        _INI_DOMAINS,
        "Domains to fail on, one per line. Empty means every custom "
        "integration, which is what a repository holding one integration "
        "wants; name domains only if the tests deliberately load somebody "
        "else's custom integration too.",
        type="linelist",
        default=[],
    )


class _ReportCollector(logging.Handler):
    """Collect the reports that blame a custom integration under test."""

    def __init__(self, domains: frozenset[str]) -> None:
        """Watch `domains`, or every custom integration when it is empty."""
        super().__init__()
        self._domains = domains
        self.reports: list[str] = []

    def emit(self, record: logging.LogRecord) -> None:
        """Keep `record` if it is a report about a watched integration."""
        args = record.args
        if not isinstance(args, tuple) or len(args) <= _DOMAIN_ARG:
            return
        if args[_KIND_ARG] != _CUSTOM_KIND:
            return
        if self._domains and args[_DOMAIN_ARG] not in self._domains:
            return
        self.reports.append(record.getMessage())


@pytest.fixture(autouse=True)
def fail_on_deprecation_report(request: pytest.FixtureRequest) -> Generator[None]:
    """
    Turn Home Assistant's reports about this integration into test failures.

    Reports name the file, the line and the source line that triggered them,
    so the failure says where to look without a traceback.

    Every test that reaches a reported call fails, not only the first: Home
    Assistant deduplicates reports by call site, but `reset_globals` clears
    that set after each test, so each test starts able to see its own.
    """
    if not request.config.getini(_INI_ENABLED):
        yield
        return

    collector = _ReportCollector(frozenset(request.config.getini(_INI_DOMAINS)))
    logger = logging.getLogger(_FRAME_LOGGER)
    # Reports are logged at WARNING. A suite that raised the threshold above it
    # would otherwise get a check that silently passes forever, which is worse
    # than not having one.
    restore_level = logger.level if not logger.isEnabledFor(logging.WARNING) else None
    if restore_level is not None:
        logger.setLevel(logging.WARNING)
    logger.addHandler(collector)
    try:
        yield
    finally:
        logger.removeHandler(collector)
        if restore_level is not None:
            logger.setLevel(restore_level)

    if collector.reports:
        pytest.fail(
            "Home Assistant reported this integration for deprecated or "
            "incorrect API usage:\n\n" + "\n\n".join(collector.reports),
            pytrace=False,
        )

"""Tests for the deprecation-report fixture."""

import pytest

# A module inside a `custom_components/` path, which is the only thing that
# makes Home Assistant call a frame a custom integration's
# (`frame.get_integration_frame` matches on the path, nothing else). Written to
# disk rather than imported so the test does not depend on a real integration
# staying deprecated.
PROBE = '''
from homeassistant.helpers.frame import ReportBehavior, report_usage


def call_deprecated_api():
    """Report from a frame inside custom_components, as a real one would."""
    report_usage(
        "calls something deprecated",
        core_behavior=ReportBehavior.IGNORE,
        core_integration_behavior=ReportBehavior.IGNORE,
        custom_integration_behavior=ReportBehavior.LOG,
        breaks_in_ha_version="2099.1.0",
    )
'''

# `hass` is what calls `frame.async_setup`, and `report_usage` raises without
# it, so the probe test takes it even though it never touches it.
TEST_USING_PROBE = '''
from custom_components.probe_integration.probe import call_deprecated_api


async def test_calls_deprecated_api(hass):
    call_deprecated_api()
'''


def ini(*lines: str) -> str:
    """Build a sub-run ini, with what every phacc consumer already sets."""
    return "\n".join(["[pytest]", "asyncio_mode = auto", *lines]) + "\n"


@pytest.fixture
def probe(pytester: pytest.Pytester) -> None:
    """Lay down the custom integration and the test that calls into it."""
    probe_dir = pytester.path / "custom_components" / "probe_integration"
    probe_dir.mkdir(parents=True)
    (probe_dir.parent / "__init__.py").write_text("")
    (probe_dir / "__init__.py").write_text("")
    (probe_dir / "probe.py").write_text(PROBE)
    pytester.makepyfile(test_probe=TEST_USING_PROBE)


def test_fails_by_default(pytester: pytest.Pytester, probe: None) -> None:
    """A report fails the suite without anything being configured."""
    pytester.makeini(ini())
    result = pytester.runpytest_subprocess()
    # The check runs after the test body, so the report arrives as a teardown
    # error rather than a failure -- the same shape `reset_globals` already uses
    # to fail a test that serialized a mock object.
    result.assert_outcomes(passed=1, errors=1)
    # The report names what to go and fix, which is the point of surfacing it.
    result.stdout.fnmatch_lines(
        ["*probe_integration*calls something deprecated*2099.1.0*"]
    )


def test_can_be_turned_off(pytester: pytest.Pytester, probe: None) -> None:
    """An escape hatch, for a suite with a backlog of reports to work through.

    Without this, adopting a version of this package that has the check would
    be a wall rather than a to-do list for anybody holding more than one
    report.
    """
    pytester.makeini(ini("phacc_fail_on_deprecation_report = false"))
    pytester.runpytest_subprocess().assert_outcomes(passed=1)


def test_ignores_reports_about_anything_but_a_custom_integration(
    pytester: pytest.Pytester,
) -> None:
    """A report with no custom integration behind it is not this suite's bug.

    Driven through `report_usage` from a test frame, which has no integration
    in it at all -- the one case Home Assistant reports without naming a
    custom integration, rather than a record built here to look like one.
    """
    pytester.makeini(ini())
    pytester.makepyfile(
        """
        from homeassistant.helpers.frame import ReportBehavior, report_usage


        async def test_report_without_an_integration_frame(hass):
            report_usage(
                "does something core cares about",
                core_behavior=ReportBehavior.LOG,
                breaks_in_ha_version="2099.1.0",
            )
        """
    )
    pytester.runpytest_subprocess().assert_outcomes(passed=1)


def test_domains_option_narrows_what_fails(
    pytester: pytest.Pytester, probe: None
) -> None:
    """Naming other domains leaves this one's reports alone."""
    pytester.makeini(
        ini(
            "phacc_deprecation_report_domains =",
            "    some_other_integration",
        )
    )
    pytester.runpytest_subprocess().assert_outcomes(passed=1)


def test_domains_option_matches_the_reported_domain(
    pytester: pytest.Pytester, probe: None
) -> None:
    """Naming this domain fails on it, so the filter is doing the deciding."""
    pytester.makeini(
        ini(
            "phacc_deprecation_report_domains =",
            "    probe_integration",
        )
    )
    pytester.runpytest_subprocess().assert_outcomes(passed=1, errors=1)

Closes #258, which has the longer version of the reasoning.

> **Revised after self-review:** the check is now **on by default** (it was opt-in), and the generator plumbing is gone entirely — see the last section.

## The gap

`homeassistant.helpers.frame.report_usage` resolves a different behaviour per kind of caller:

| caller | behaviour | result in a test |
| --- | --- | --- |
| homeassistant/core | `core_behavior` — `ERROR` at most call sites | raises |
| a test frame, no integration in the stack | `core_behavior` via `MissingIntegrationFrame` | raises |
| **a custom integration** | `custom_integration_behavior` — **defaults to `LOG`** | logs, test passes |

Core's own suite is protected. A custom integration's cannot be. Its production code can call a deprecated helper and the suite stays green — at 100% coverage, with a dedicated test asserting exactly what that code does, because the code is *correct*, just scheduled for removal.

That is [lock_code_manager#1595](https://github.com/raman325/lock_code_manager/issues/1595): one PR migrated every `device_registry.async_get_device` call, a second PR branched before that landed and added a new block using the old calls, and the merge had nothing to conflict with. A user found it by reading their own logs. A local version of this check caught it on the first run.

## What this adds

- `src/phacc_deprecation.py` — a `pytest11` plugin: two ini options and one autouse fixture.
- `setup.py` — `py_modules` and a second entry point.
- `tests/test_deprecation.py` — five `pytester` tests.
- A README section.

Five files, no generator changes.

## On by default

A report that a custom integration called a deprecated API is a defect every time. Behind an opt-in flag it would be found only by people who already knew to look, which is the same population that does not need it.

This does change existing suites' results, so it wants a minor version bump under your version strategy. The escape hatch makes adoption a to-do list rather than a wall:

```ini
[pytest]
asyncio_mode = auto
phacc_fail_on_deprecation_report = false
```

`phacc_deprecation_report_domains` narrows it instead, for a repo whose tests deliberately load someone else's custom integration.

This repo's own suite now runs with the check on and **no** configuration line, so `simple_integration` is clean by demonstration rather than by assertion.

## No generator changes

`generate_phacc` wipes `src/pytest_homeassistant_custom_component`, not all of `src/` — so a module *beside* that directory survives regeneration untouched. `src/phacc_deprecation.py` plus `py_modules=["phacc_deprecation"]` is the entire mechanism.

That removed, versus the first revision: the `extras/` directory, two `const.py` entries, a copy step in `generate_phacc.py`, and a generated copy that had to be committed because `publish.yml` builds from the checkout without regenerating. I verified it by replaying the generator's `shutil.rmtree(PACKAGE_DIR)` / `os.mkdir` against a copy of `src/`: the package directory is emptied and the module is still there.

The one thing worth your opinion is the name. It has to live outside the regenerated directory, so it is a second top-level importable name rather than `pytest_homeassistant_custom_component.deprecation`. Happy to rename it to whatever you prefer.

## Other decisions worth your eyes

**A log handler, not a patch of `report_usage`.** Patching would be incomplete and semantically wrong — about 10 modules do `from homeassistant.helpers.frame import report_usage`, so a module-attribute patch misses them, and at least one call site deliberately passes `custom_integration_behavior=ReportBehavior.IGNORE`, which forcing `ERROR` would override. A handler also survives a broad `except Exception` in the code under test, where a raised exception would be swallowed and the check would silently pass.

**Reports recognised from `record.args`, not the message text.** Both `_LOGGER.log` call sites in `frame.py` pass the integration kind first and the domain second, so the check reads those rather than matching wording that has been reworded before.

**Fails after `yield`,** so it surfaces as a teardown error rather than a failure. That is the same shape `reset_globals` already uses to fail a test that serialized a mock object; the tests assert `passed=1, errors=1` and say why.

## Verification

Full suite green, 12 passed, with the check on and unconfigured:

- a report fails the suite with nothing configured, and the output names the integration, file and line
- `phacc_fail_on_deprecation_report = false` turns it off
- a report with no custom integration behind it (driven through `report_usage` from a test frame, not a hand-built log record) does not fail
- the domain filter both narrows and matches

This does change existing suites' results, so it wants a minor version bump under your version strategy. The escape hatch makes adoption a to-do list rather than a wall:

```ini
[pytest]
asyncio_mode = auto
phacc_fail_on_deprecation_report = false
```

`phacc_deprecation_report_domains` narrows it instead, for a repo whose tests deliberately load someone else's custom integration.

This repo's own suite now runs with the check on and **no** configuration line, so `simple_integration` is clean by demonstration rather than by assertion.

## No generator changes

`generate_phacc` wipes `src/pytest_homeassistant_custom_component`, not all of `src/` — so a module *beside* that directory survives regeneration untouched. `src/phacc_deprecation.py` plus `py_modules=["phacc_deprecation"]` is the entire mechanism.

That removed, versus the first revision: the `extras/` directory, two `const.py` entries, a copy step in `generate_phacc.py`, and a generated copy that had to be committed because `publish.yml` builds from the checkout without regenerating. I verified it by replaying the generator's `shutil.rmtree(PACKAGE_DIR)` / `os.mkdir` against a copy of `src/`: the package directory is emptied and the module is still there.

The one thing worth your opinion is the name. It has to live outside the regenerated directory, so it is a second top-level importable name rather than `pytest_homeassistant_custom_component.deprecation`. Happy to rename it to whatever you prefer.

## Other decisions worth your eyes

**A log handler, not a patch of `report_usage`.** Patching would be incomplete and semantically wrong — about 10 modules do `from homeassistant.helpers.frame import report_usage`, so a module-attribute patch misses them, and at least one call site deliberately passes `custom_integration_behavior=ReportBehavior.IGNORE`, which forcing `ERROR` would override. A handler also survives a broad `except Exception` in the code under test, where a raised exception would be swallowed and the check would silently pass.

**Reports recognised from `record.args`, not the message text.** Both `_LOGGER.log` call sites in `frame.py` pass the integration kind first and the domain second, so the check reads those rather than matching wording that has been reworded before.

**Fails after `yield`,** so it surfaces as a teardown error rather than a failure. That is the same shape `reset_globals` already uses to fail a test that serialized a mock object; the tests assert `passed=1, errors=1` and say why.

## Verification

Full suite green, 12 passed, with the check on and unconfigured:

- a report fails the suite with nothing configured, and the output names the integration, file and line
- `phacc_fail_on_deprecation_report = false` turns it off
- a report with no custom integration behind it (driven through `report_usage` from a test frame, not a hand-built log record) does not fail
- the domain filter both narrows and matches

## #1273 and #1588 — [PR #1605](https://github.com/raman325/lock_code_manager/pull/1605)

Neither was a test failure. **Both died at `uv pip install`, before pytest ran** — the `Python / Pytest (3.14)` red X and the codecov error underneath it are both downstream of a resolver conflict.

```
#1273: pytest-homeassistant-custom-component==0.13.346 depends on pytest==9.0.3
       and you require pytest>=9.1.1 → unsatisfiable
#1588: homeassistant>=2026.9.4 depends on zeroconf==0.151.1
       and you require zeroconf==0.151.3 → unsatisfiable
```

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The useful question was *which* of the 16 packages in the `homeassistant` dependabot group the HA wheel actually constrains. Answer: **exactly one, `zeroconf`.** The rest are integration deps pinned in HA *manifests*, which never reach the wheel's `Requires-Dist` — so we have to mirror those ourselves, and dependabot bumping them is legitimate.
- That flips the fix for each PR. `zeroconf` was a *duplicate* of a pin we don't own, added back in #77, imported by nothing — so the line comes out and the resolver takes HA's version (confirmed: it resolved to 0.151.1 on its own). `pytest` is pinned **exactly** by phacc because phacc carries all of HA core's test requirements, so no bump can ever resolve — that one needs `ignore`, not a fix. #1273 was never going to go green; it just needed someone to say so.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

The other seven updates in #1588 are taken as proposed. Verified in a scratch venv (your `.venv` untouched): `homeassistant==2026.9.4`, `zha==2.2.2`, `zigpy==2.2.0`, `zha-quirks==2.2.2`, `aioesphomeapi==46.6.0`, `debugpy==1.8.22`, `phacc==0.13.367` — **full suite 2450 passed, 3 skipped**. zigpy 2.2.0 changes struct bitfield endianness, so the ZHA provider tests were the real risk; they pass. Ruff, Mypy, Hassfest, HACS green; the Pytest job is still running and I'm waiting on it.

Both dependabot PRs should close themselves once it re-evaluates — worth a glance in case they need closing by hand.

## phcc — both points taken, [PR #259](https://github.com/MatthewFlamm/pytest-homeassistant-custom-component/pull/259) revised

**On by default**, with `phacc_fail_on_deprecation_report = false` as the escape hatch for a suite with a backlog. phcc's own suite now runs with the check on and *no* config line, so `simple_integration` is clean by demonstration. Flagged in the PR that this warrants a minor version bump under their strategy.

**You were right about the boilerplate, and the reason is embarrassing in a useful way:** `generate_phacc` runs `rmtree` on `src/pytest_homeassistant_custom_component`, not on `src/`. A module *beside* that directory survives regeneration untouched. So `src/phacc_deprecation.py` + `py_modules` is the entire mechanism — **zero generator changes**.

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| files in diff | 9 | 5 |
| `extras/` dir, `const.py` entries, copy step | yes | gone |
| committed generated copy | required | gone |
